title.narrative: Activity under preparation ACCESS:Strengthening Services, Natural Resource Management and Social Cohesion in Northern Ghana

description.narrative: This action intends to reduce the risk of spillover of conflict and radicalisation in northern Ghana by addressing the root causes of instability: marginalization, lack of services and the degradation of land and natural resources. Following an integrated territorial approach, the initiative strengthens (i) access to and quality of basic services and productive assets; (ii) land and natural resource management; and (iii) participatory local governance, strengthening the inclusion of marginalized groups (including women, youth, and transhumant communities)in the sustainable management of their territory.Evidence from neighbouring countries shows that extremist groups exploit vulnerabilities and local grievances to radicalise marginalised populations.[1] While state narratives often frame extremism as an external threat, local perspectives highlight internal socio-economic and political factors as key drivers that expose desperate populations to radicalisation. This Action will complement ongoing and planned EU interventions on security, cross-border cooperation, and peacebuilding in Ghana, thereby reinforcing EU as a comprehensive stakeholder in the fight against violent extremism.Northern Ghana, the more arid part of the country, is characterized as a poverty hotspot where recent trends show a significant increase in poverty rates despite national stagnation. This regional divide is reflected in a severe scarcity of basic services; for instance, less than 50 percent of the population in many northern districts has access to electricity, and open defecation remains a persistent challenge with rates exceeding 50 percent in five northern regions. Beyond infrastructure, the gap extends to essential human services: in the Upper West region, only 3 percent of students pass the national Basic Education Certificate Examination, compared to nearly two-thirds in Greater Accra. Furthermore, healthcare accessibility remains a major hurdle, as more than 20 percent of northern residents must travel over 30 minutes for water, while many women in the North live in areas where reaching the nearest health facility can take over an hourThe regional disparity is rooted in historical neglect and state policies that favoured southern economic growth, particularly cocoa production and gold mining, over northern interests. Consequently, the northern zone has historically served as a labour reserve for the south.In addition, Ghana is facing an unprecedented depletion of natural resources that the state is failing to address. This loss of natural capital locks marginalized rural populations into a cycle of unsustainable land-use practices and declining incomes. Ultimately, this environmental degradation fuels conflict over increasingly scarce resources, further deepening the exclusion of northern communities and increasing the risk of spill over of conflict and radicalisation.
